GOWDA: Goal-oriented Web Documents Querying tool

Bahareh Zarei

Technische Universität Chemnitz

Chemnitz, Saxony

bahareh.zarei@informatik.tu-chemnitz.de

Martin Gaedke

Technische Universität Chemnitz

Chemnitz, Saxony

martin.gaedke@informatik.tu-chemnitz.de

ABSTRACT
Each day, a vast amount of data is published on the web. In addi-
tion, the rate at which content is being published is growing, which
has the potential to overwhelm users, particularly those who are
technically unskilled. Furthermore, users from various domains
of expertise face challenges when trying to retrieve the data they
require. They may rely on IT experts, but these experts have limited
knowledge of individual domains, making data extraction a time-
consuming and error-prone task. It would be beneficial if domain
experts were able to retrieve needed data and create relatively com-
plex queries on top of web documents. The existing query solutions
either are limited to a specific domain or require beginning with a
predefined knowledge base or sample ontologies. To address these
limitations, we propose a goal-oriented platform that enables users
to easily extract data from web documents. This platform enables
users to express their goals in natural language, after which the
platform elicits the corresponding result type using the algorithm
proposed. The platform also applies the concept of ontology to
semantically improve search results. To retrieve the most relevant
results from web documents, the segments of a user’s query are
mapped to the entities of the ontology. Two types of ontologies are
used: goal ontologies and domain-specific ones, which comprise
domain concepts and the relationships among them. In addition,
the platform helps domain experts to generate the domain ontolo-
gies that will be used to extract data from web documents. Placing
ontologies at the center of the approach integrates a level of seman-
tics into the platform, resulting in more-precise output. The main
contributions of this research are that it provides a goal-oriented
platform for extracting data from web documents and integrates
ontology-based development into web-document searches.

1 INTRODUCTION
The World Wide Web provides access to a vast amount of unstruc-
tured or semi-structured information in various forms, including
web pages, research papers, scholarly documents, and e-books. The
current volume and rate of increase of these web documents causes
major problems for unskilled users attempting to retrieve the exact
data they need[12]. Conventional approaches to searching web
documents, including keyword-based or form-based techniques,
are not sufficiently expressive to enable users to formulate complex
queries, and they also present limitations regarding identifying and
returning the correct data. Although using web query languages, in-
cluding XQuery and WebSQL, increases the expressiveness to some
extent, these languages require users to have a certain amount
of technical knowledge[16]. Another limitation of conventional
search methods is that they ignore the domain and semantics of
words. A word’s semantics may change depending on the domain
in which it is used. For example, the word “cell” means “basic unit
of life” in the biology domain and “area of radio coverage” in the
cellular-network domain. To increase the precision of query results,
it is essential to consider the user’s domain.

To address the above-mentioned problems, we propose a goal-
oriented approach to finding the exact web data that users need
using ontology-based searches. Domain knowledge can be descri-
bed in the form of an ontology consisting of a structured set of
domain entities and the relationships among them[11]. The advan-
tages of integrating ontologies into web searches include increased
precision, easier access to the data exacted, and the extraction of
concepts instead of only keywords[14]. Furthermore, the proposed
platform, GOWDA, enables users to express their intentions in
natural language in the form of goal statements, which helps naive
users to create reasonable search queries. A goal can be achieved
through a set of actions and their corresponding results. This fe-
ature contributes to the solution’s simplicity and expressiveness.
In addition, to overcome the limitations imposed by the semantic
ambiguity of words, the approach integrates domain ontologies
as a middleware layer. After the type of the results is identified,
the goals’ entities, including subgoals and tasks, are mapped to
the domain ontologies, which the GOWDA platform also enables
domain experts to generate.

Because generating ontologies manually is time consuming, we
propose a semi-automatic technique for generating domain-specific
ontologies for any given domain. This method asks domain experts
to first prepare a large dataset of domain-related documents and

DocEng ’18, August 28–31, 2018, Halifax, NS, Canada

B. Zarei and M. Gaedke

then uses this dataset to identify the main domain entities and the
relationships among them. Then, the Word2vec algorithm 1 is used
to extract these entities. After each step, the domain experts are
asked to refine the output.

This remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section
2 presents an overview of similar approaches. Section 3 describes
the proposed approach in detail and presents the GOWDA plat-
form’s overall architecture. Section 4 validates the feasibility of the
proposed approach. Section 5 presents conclusions and discusses
potential future improvements.

2 RELATED WORK
In recent years, extracting data from web documents has received
considerable research attention. A wide spectrum of domains can
benefit from improvements to the processes of creating queries
and extracting knowledge from web documents. One core domain
is the enterprise one, which requires business users to have ad-
hoc access to data. An example of an enterprise application with a
focus on business intelligence was presented by [17] who used a
domain-specific, ontology-based architecture to integrate data from
heterogeneous sources with the help of an ontology model, Business
Ontology (BO), which contained business-related concepts. The
Semantic Query Designer on the top layer, or application layer, of
the architecture enabled users to visually formulate the query, and
then mapping between the BO and the data-storage layer occurred.
The proposed approach is similar to [17] in that ontology-based
development is a central aspect of it. Furthermore, the proposed
approach enables interaction based on natural language.

Early practices in this area focused on domain-specific languages
to define rules for data extraction, including the solutions provided
by [9, 10, 13]. in which the quality of the extraction rules defined
by the operators determined the quality of the data extracted.

Other solutions have used machine-learning techniques, inclu-
ding supervised or semi-supervised methods. In such solutions, the
domain expert first creates a sample dataset from various web docu-
ments and trains the tool on it, after this training phase the tool can
extract data [6]. Approaches such as that of [1, 3, 4] rely on these
machine-learning techniques, meaning that they necessarily in-
volve creation of large training datasets, which is a time-consuming
task for domain experts.

GATE [2] is a well-known framework that relies on machine-
learning techniques to extract information and that provides a
rich toolkit for natural language processing and data mining. The
proposed approach differs from GATE in that it takes into account
the semantic meaning of words.

Other solution category which gains popularity during the recent
years, is Natural-language interfaces such as Apple’s Siri 2, Cortana
3 and Amazon’s Alexa 4. The proposed is in this category.

This approach can be classified as an ontology-based semantic
search technique. In such techniques, the meaning of the query is
important, rather than the syntax of the keywords used [11]. [8, 14–
16, 18] presents some ontology-based practices. The main aspect

that differentiates the GOWDA approach from existing ontology-
based practices is that the GOWDA approach integrates a goal
ontology layer to better address the user’s needs and to enable the

3 GOWDA FRAMEWORK AND

IMPLEMENTATION

We propose a goal-oriented approach to answer users’ queries effi-
ciently. Goal-oriented designs aim to create a more usable platform
by focusing on the users’ goals rather than their tasks [5]. As Fi-
gure 1. shows, the GOWDA architecture comprises three main
components. The first is the Natural Language Processing (NLP)
component, which is responsible for translating a user’s goal into
a reasonable query by performing Part of speech (POS) tagging
and goal-ontology mapping. This component is implemented using
the Python Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK) library. The second
component is the goal ontology, which is responsible for mapping
the output of the NLP component to the goal ontology (goal and
result). Then, after the type of results that the user is querying,
such as a person, a location, or any domain-dependent concept, is
identified, mapping to the domain ontology is performed. The goal
ontology is implemented in Protege 5, an open-source ontology
editor, which is also used to build the knowledge base.

The third architecture component is mapping from the back-
ground knowledge in the form of ontology to the web documents.
Each related web page is semantically annotated according to the
domain ontology. Semantic annotations are a formal way of descri-
bing the knowledge contained in a web document and are in the
form of RDF files that can be mapped against the domain ontology
to extract the instances of each entity. For instance, ‘Jane Wilson’
and ‘TU Chemnitz’ are two instances extracted from a web page and
can be mapped to the student and university entities, respectively,
from the education domain ontology.

As an example, the user first types into the text field “Who is
working in Web engineering?” as the goal. Based on the output of
the NLP component, “Who” is tagged as WP, which refers to the
WH pronoun and corresponds to a person’s name. In this example,
the desired result is the names of people working in the “web
engineering” field, so, the results should be of type DO:person (DO
is for entities in the domain ontology). The SPARQL query language
returns as the results all the entities that are labeled as person and
that have the value “web engineering” in their field.
4 ONTOLOGY GENERATION
In order for the platform to be usable by various domains, their
corresponding domain ontologies must be integrated into the plat-
form. In this approach, generating ontologies includes three steps:
preprocessing, concept extraction, and relationship extraction. As
the primary task, the domain experts upload sample domain-related
documents to serve as the text corpus in later steps. Next, to prepare
this corpus for step 2, preprocessing is performed, which consists
of removing special characters and stop words, the latter being
defined as frequently used words that carry no important meaning,
including ‘an’, ‘and’, and ‘for.’ Removing such words provides a
more accurate training set for use in step 2, concept extraction,
5https://protege.stanford.edu/

GOWDA: Goal-oriented Web Documents Querying tool

DocEng ’18, August 28–31, 2018, Halifax, NS, Canada

Figure 1: Platform overall architecture.

which extracts the keywords according to the word’s semantic con-
cept using the Word2vec algorithm, a two-layer neural-network
algorithm. Word2vec has been selected for use in the proposed
approach because of its unique performance in providing syntactic
and semantic measurements of words [19]. The word2vec algorithm
is trained on a large corpus of text and forms a vector space repre-
sentation of this corpus, onto which input words are mapped. To
each word in the corpus, word2vec assigns a vector which later can
be used to compute the similarity between words and sentences.
The proposed approach uses the Python genism library 6for im-
plementing the Word2vec algorithm. Step 2, Concept Extraction,
extracts the main keywords from the corpus. Preparatory to this,
the domain expert identifies a small set of seed concepts, and then,
the algorithm extracts new concept candidates based on each con-
cept in this set. After each iteration, the domain expert confirms the
relevant extracted terms as key concepts and deletes the irrelevant
ones. To increase the quality of the model produced, the training
phase tunes two parameters, size and min_count. The size para-
meter is the dimensions of the feature vectors, and the min_count
sets the minimum frequency. For example, min count = 3 tells the
algorithm to ignore all words with a frequency lower than 3. The
values used for these parameters depend on the size of the training
corpus.

Finally, step 3, relationship extraction, consists of identifying
all (entity, relationship, entity) tuples from which entities already
were extracted during step 2. The overall approach to relationship
extraction is to first split the text into sentences and then to tag
each sentence with POS tags, including nouns, verbs, adjectives,
etc. To explore the semantic relationships among the concepts, one
possible approach is the self-supervised one[7], which identifies
the textual patterns that occur between key concepts. However, our
approach considers the verbs linking two concepts as relationships.
The detailed procedures are shown in Figure 2.

5 VALIDATION
This section demonstrates the feasibility of our approach. For this
demonstration, we chose the traveling domain and presented a
specific scenario. First, we constructed an ontology based on the
corpus provided by the domain expert, which consisted of 12,917
sentences and included data regarding flight, hotel and car rental
histories. The corpus contains short sentences and long textual
descriptions. Using a set of 10 seed words provided the algorithm
with 64% precision in identifying the key concepts. The output

6https://radimrehurek.com/gensim/

Figure 2: Ontology generation algorithms.

domain ontology was stored in RDF format in the form of triples
<N1, P, N2>, for example: <hotel, isLocatedIn, city>.

Figure 3. illustrates the detailed steps for addressing the query
“What are the addresses of hotels located in Berlin that have 4-star
ratings?”. According to the NLP component, the combination of
“What” as a WH pronoun and the noun “addresses” as a location
reference signified that to fulfill the user’s goal, the result should
consist of instances of the domain entity. The entity type for address
was defined as location in the domain ontology.

The next step identified the key terms in the query and each
term’s corresponding POS tags. To map these terms to the corre-
sponding entities in the domain ontology, a query was run on this
ontology. The nouns were mapped to the classes, and the verbs
were presented as relationships among classes. For each class, there
was a list of interchangeable words to which the user’s query terms
could be mapped. For instance, “accommodation” was listed as an
interchangeable word for the class hotel, so, when “accommoda-
tion” was used in the query, the platform mapped it to the class
hotel. After the query’s key terms were matched to instances of

On  some  end-user  programming  constructs  and  their 
understandability

Michał Ma ´ckowiak

Keywords: 
End-user programming 
Code understanding 
Spreadsheets 

Context : End-user programming is becoming more and more important. However, existing programming 
paradigms and the languages based on them seem far-removed from what end-user programmers would 
need, especially in the area of Management Information. 

Objective : To evaluate the understandability of a set of programming constructs based on the spreadsheet 
metaphor from the point of view of end-user programmers in the context of Management Information. 
The examined set comprises single assignment with exemplary computations, data-driven iterations, se- 
lection by colours, and read-write heads (we refer to this as Board Programming ). 

Method:  A series of experiments was performed with students of Management Engineering, split into 
an experimental group and a control group. Each participant was given a piece of code expressed ei- 
ther with the proposed programming construct (experimental group) or its classical counterpart (con- 
trol group). Their task was to predict the results. For the purpose of evaluation, the FACT indicators of 
understandability (First attempt failure rate, Attempt number, Cancellation ratio, prediction Time) were 
proposed and measured. 

Results:  Three of the four examined features, i.e. single assignment with exemplary computations, data- 
driven iterations, and read-write heads, proved to increase understandability of the chosen programs with 
regard to three out of the four FACT indicators, and these results were statistically signiﬁcant. Selection 
by colours was not as effective as expected: the FACT indicator values were improved by that feature, but 
the difference was not statistically signiﬁcant. 

Conclusions:  The described programming constructs appear to be an interesting option when designing 
an end-user programming language for domain experts in the ﬁeld of Management Information.

1. Introduction 

For many years there has been a shortage of computer experts, 
including programmers. According to some sources, in the US the 
annual growth in available jobs is almost three times higher than 
the rate of students graduating with bachelor’s degrees in Com- 
puter Science ( Partovi, 2014 ). In the Netherlands a shortage of pro- 
grammers  is  expected  to  be  the  main  factor  driving  up  wages 
( Bouman, 2016 ). Globally, IT vacancies (i.e. programmers, database 
experts, etc.) are the second hardest to ﬁll ( ManpowerGroup, 2016 ). 
When  there  is  a  shortage  of  a  resource,  the  question  arises 
whether the resource is used rationally and whether there exists

any substitute. As regards programmers, one can consider hobbyists 
and end users as potential substitutes for professional software de- 
velopers. A worldwide study performed by IDC (2014) shows that 
in addition to 11 million professional software developers there are 
about 7.5 million hobbyists. According to other data ( Scaﬃdi et al., 
2005 ), in the US the ratio of professional programmers to end-user 
programmers is 3 to 55. 

There are many problems that do not require deep program- 
ming skills but do require deep domain knowledge. In such a con- 
text an end-user programmer (a person who creates programs for 
herself ( Ko et al., 2011 )) could be the right choice. This is especially 
true in the area of management information, where it is common 
to make use of MS Excel, which combines the power of a data grid 
interface with the possibility of programming macros in Visual Ba- 
sic for Applications (VBA). These features make spreadsheet appli- 
cations extremely popular. For instance, as reported by Panko and 
Port (2012) , a single bank can have about 9 million MS Excel ﬁles 

M. Ma ´ckowiak et al. / The Journal of Systems and Software 142 (2018) 206–222 

207 

in use (!). Unfortunately, spreadsheets have their weaknesses too. 
According to Business Insider (2013) , JP Morgan has lost US$6 bil- 
lion due to bugs in their Value-at-Risk model implemented with 
spreadsheets. One could blame end users and their carelessness, 
but  the  real  culprit  may  be  the  gap  between  the  very  easy-to- 
use data grid interface and the hard-to-program macros in Visual 
Basic. In many cases, they would prefer to use complex formulae 
and copy-pasting instead of writing a macro which might fail when 
some modiﬁcations to the calculations are introduced. 

Shortage of professional programmers and problems of ﬁnan- 
cial  experts  with  spreadsheets  are  not  the  only  motivations  for 
working  on  improving  languages  and  environments  for  end-user 
programming.  This  approach  gives  users  empowerment  and  can 
lead  to  better  use  of  their  domain  knowledge.  More  usage  con- 
texts  for  end-user  programming  can  be  found,  for  instance,  in 
Ko et al. (2011) . 

To  be  more  effective,  domain  experts  would  need  program- 
ming constructs that are both easy to use and supportive in writ- 
ing  business  utilities,  i.e.  small  programs  that  are  useful  in  the 
business environment of a given domain expert (e.g. value-at-risk 
models). MS Excel is a solution, but far from an ideal one. Some 
attempts  to  improve  the  situation  have  already  been  made  (e.g. 
Jones et al. (2003) , Sestoft and Sørensen (2013) ), but it seems that 
there is still plenty of space for improvement, and it is worthwhile 
to consider new ideas. 

In  this  paper,  four  end-user  programming  constructs  are 
proposed  and  examined.  They  form  an  end-user  programming 
paradigm  which  we  call  Board  Programming .  It  is  based  on  the 
metaphor of spreadsheets. As a consequence, Board Programming 
offers to the programmer exemplary computations and—to facili- 
tate understanding—it does not allow to overwrite data (that ap- 
proach is known as single assignment ). Moreover, it uses so-called 
index arrays instead of loops (that is typical for spreadsheet-like 
computations) and allows to use colours to select data (it is a kind 
of complement to conditional formatting which is available in Ex- 
cel). Board Programming is designed to be useful for end-user pro- 
grammers (more precisely, junior managers) working in the area of 
management information. 

The main topic of the paper is to validate the understandabil- 
ity of the proposed constructs experimentally. Following the rapid 
prototyping approach ( Myers et al., 2016 ), we want to gather early 
feedback and made a decision based on evidence ( Steﬁk and Ha- 
nenberg, 2017 ) which of them should be included in the designed 
language. 

The  paper  is  organised  in  the  following  way.  Firstly,  in 
Section 2 , the notion of understandability is deﬁned, and a set of 
performance indicators is proposed. As the evaluation of the pro- 
posed programming constructs was performed by a series of very 
similar experiments, in Section 3 the experimental framework (the 
common part of all of the experiments) is described. Because of 
this, the experimental parts of the subsequent sections are quite 
short and mainly present the results. The proposed programming 
constructs are discussed in Sections 4 –7 . Each of the sections con- 
tains a description of the programming construct, an example, a 
short overview of related work, and the results of the experimental 
evaluation (i.e. performance indicators). Finally, Section 8 presents 
several acceptance indicators of the proposed paradigm, obtained 
from the participants in the experiments (these data show how far 
the they are willing to use a programming language based on the 
proposed constructs), as well as conclusions and future work. 

Deﬁnition 1. The understandability of a set of programming con- 
structs is the degree of ease of predicting the results of computa- 
tions deﬁned by means of those constructs. 

JUSTIFICATION. The  proposed  deﬁnition  appears  similar  to  the 
deﬁnitions of understandability given by Grubb and Takang (2003) : 

Program understandability is the ease with which the program can 
be understood—that is, the ability to determine what a program 
does and how it works by reading its source code and accompany- 
ing documentation. 

and by Patig (2008) : 

Understandability  can  be  seen  as  [...]  an  aspect  of  ease  of  use, 
namely  the  effort  r equir ed  t o  r ead  and  corr ectly  interpr et  some 
model. 

If a person can predict the results of a given computation (e.g. 
the result of a function for given values of input parameters), then 
that  person  certainly  understands  that  piece  of  code.  The  oppo- 
site implication is also true, provided that the input does not re- 
sult in over-complicated computations (for example, numbers with 
many digits in the fraction part can be diﬃcult for a human to 
cope with). 

It may be claimed that the deﬁnition of understandability given 
above  strongly  depends  on  the  input  data:  time  complexity  de- 
pends on the size of the input data. If the time complexity is high, 
it is not easy to predict the results, even if the code itself is fairly 
simple. This is indeed true in general, but the research reported 
here has the form of a comparative study: there will always be a 
pair of sets of programming constructs (e.g. Visual Basic vs. new 
programming  constructs),  and  we  will  be  investigating  whether 
one set is easier to understand than the other. In this context, the 
impact of input data can be neglected, as both the algorithm and 
the input data will always be the same for the experimental and 
control groups. 

However, when conducting this type of experiment it is impor- 
tant to use input data that do not require a large number of man- 
ual computations—otherwise, the time spent by a participant on 
calculations would be considerably greater than the time necessary 
to understand the code. This would obscure the difference between 
the experimental and the control version. 

Assumption  1. The  understandability  of  a  set  of  programming 
constructs, when evaluated by a group of people, can be described 
with the following performance indicators (we call them the FACT 
indicators of understandability): 
• F — ﬁrst attempt failure ratio: the percentage of people (partic- 
ipants) who fail at the ﬁrst attempt to predict the results of a 
computation deﬁned by means of a given set of programming 
constructs; 

• A — attempt number: the average number of attempts needed 
to predict the correct results of computations deﬁned by code

• C — cancellation ratio: the percentage of participants who are

• T — prediction time: the average time used by participants to 
predict the results of a computation deﬁned by code composed 
of the analysed programming constructs. 

2. Understandability and its indicators 

In  the  context  of  programming  constructs,  understandability 

can be deﬁned as follows. 

JUSTIFICATION. Prediction time, T , seems the most important and 
natural indicator of understandability. For computational tasks per- 
formed by a human, one can assume that the mental process as a 
whole is split into two types of activities: understanding a given 

208 

M. Ma ´ckowiak et al. / The Journal of Systems and Software 142 (2018) 206–222 

piece of code (what I have to do in a given step) and perform- 
ing the actual calculations. If there are two groups of programmers 
and both of them are given what is in fact the same computational 
task (in the sense of arithmetical calculations, e.g. computing the 
value of the same or very similar polynomials), but these compu- 
tations are described with different programming constructs, then 
the time spent on arithmetical calculations will be on average the 
same or very similar for both groups, and any difference in pre- 
diction time can be attributed to the activity of understanding the 
code. Thus, prediction time, T , seems a good indicator of under- 
standability. 

The second important understandability indicator is the cancel- 
lation  ratio,  C .  It  is  especially  important  in  the  context  of  con- 
trolled  experiments  with  limited  time.  Some  participants  would 
need more time than that allotted for the experiment. If for one 
group the cancellation ratio is higher than for the other, it proba- 
bly means that their code was more diﬃcult to understand. 

The two remaining indicators—ﬁrst attempt failure ratio ( F ) and 
attempts  number  ( A )—are  somewhat  auxiliary,  but  can  still  pro- 
vide valuable insight. We may expect that if two groups of par- 
ticipants were given the same computation tasks expressed using 
different programming constructs, then the group for which F and 
A are lower had fewer problems in understanding the program. 

3. Evaluation framework 

The programming constructs discussed in the subsequent sec- 
tions  were  evaluated  experimentally  with  the  following  goal  in 
mind (here we used the goal description template proposed in the 
Goal Question Metric approach, van Solingen et al. (2002) ): 

Goal 1. The purpose of the programming experiments was to eval- 
uate the understandability of the proposed end-user programming 
constructs  (i.e.  single  assignment  with  exemplary  computations, 
data-driven indices, selection by colours, and read-write heads) in 
terms of the FACT indicators and in the context of a research fund- 
ing  body  wishing  to  know  whether  it  makes  sense  to  invest  in 
the development of a programming language and IDE based on the 
proposed constructs (i.e. Board Programming). 

The  evaluation  mentioned  in  Goal  1  was  performed  by  com- 
paring the proposed programming constructs with their classical 
counterparts—mainly with the corresponding code written in Vi- 
sual  Basic.  There  were  three  reasons  for  choosing  this  program- 
ming language. Firstly, using the proposed programming constructs 
could be perceived as an alternative to writing macros in Visual 
Basic  to  solve  some  of  the  more  complex  problems  that  cannot 
be  easily  solved  solely  using  the  data  grid  interfaces  offered  by 
spreadsheet applications. Secondly, it was a programming language 
with which the persons participating in the experiments were fa- 
miliar.  Since  they  were  novice  end-user  programmers  with  not 
much experience, we thought it would be better to focus on the 
language they already knew instead of teaching them a new one. 
Finally, the programs which were used in the experiments were 
built upon a limited set of basic constructs which often are very 
similar in different programming languages (e.g, for loops, if state- 
ments, arrays). 

To evaluate the proposed programming constructs a series of 
controlled experiments were conducted, all with very similar de- 
signs. For this reason, we shall describe their common part here as 
the evaluation framework . 

3.1. Experiment design 

The experiments involved the following roles: lecturer (the per- 
son in this role was to provide an introductory lecture—one of the 
authors did this), observers (the purpose of this role was to make 

sure that there was no cheating during the experiments—two au- 
thors acted as observers), and participants split into experimental 
and control groups. 

Participants.  The participants were 114 ﬁrst-year students of the 
bachelor degree programme in Management Engineering at Poznan 
University of Technology. A list of the courses which may have en- 
hanced their mathematical and computational skills is presented 
in Tab. 1 . 

The experiments were conducted during the second half of the 
Information Technology in Management course (the second semester 
of the curriculum) in the academic years 2014/2015 and 2015/2016. 
During the ﬁrst experimental session in 2015, we conducted the 
experiment presented in Section 5 , while the three remaining ex- 
periments took place during a single session in 2016. In the lat- 
ter session, the students solved tasks in the order in which they 
are presented in the following sections of the paper. The number 
of participants in these three experiments decreased from task to 
task, as some of the them were not able to provide answers for the 
preceding tasks before the allotted time ran out (the ﬁrst task was 
done by 44 participants, the sceond—36, and the last—28). 

Before  starting  the  experiments,  the  participants  had  already 
undergone (during their study programme) an introduction to pro- 
gramming in Visual Basic: 10 hours of lectures and 15 hours of lab- 
oratory classes. The course was conducted by regular tutors who 
were not involved either in the experiments or in the development 
of the constructs presented in this paper. The students attended to 
the experiments during their regular classes. Their results did not 
affect their grades. 

Execution scenario.  The procedure used in each of the experimen- 
tal sessions consisted of the following steps: 

1. Lecture. This lasted for 90 minutes and consisted of (1) an intro- 
duction to end-user programming, (2) a review of Visual Basic 
features, (3) an explanation of the programming concepts for 
end-users  presented in  this  paper,  and  (4)  information about 
the experiment. The presentation included 103 slides: 23 about 
the end-user programming problem, 41 about Visual Basic, 36 
about  Board  Programming,  and  3  about  the  experiment.  The 
lecture was attended by a majority of the prospective partici- 
pants. 

2. Group  selection.  We  used  random  stratiﬁed  sampling  to  form 
the experimental and control groups. We asked the tutors of 
the course to indicate those participants who were very good 
at programming and those who were very slow with program- 
ming  assignments.  Half  of  the  very  good  programmers  were 
randomly  assigned  to  the  experimental  group,  and  the  other 
half to the control group. The same was done with the slow 
programmers, and with those who were not identiﬁed as either 
very good or slow. 

3. Experiment. A week after the lecture the main part of the exper- 
iment took place. It was allotted 100 minutes, and it consisted 
of the following parts: 
(a) Review mini-lecture. The lecturer provided a short review of 
the material presented during the lecture (ca. 30 minutes). 
It covered both Visual Basic (8 slides) and the end-user pro- 
gramming concepts discussed (27 slides). Also, some tech- 
nical aspects were explained (how to log in to the system, 
where to ﬁnd the slides used during the lecture, how to pro- 
vide feedback, etc.). All of the participants attended this lec- 
ture. 

(b) Warm-up.  Two  exemplary  assignments  were  presented  to 
each participant concerning the Factorial function (in Visual 
Basic) and the Power function (in Board Programming). The 
subjects worked in the same way as described in the next

During the experiment, all the participants spent ca. 30 minutes 
on the review mini-lecture. Next, they worked 10 minutes (on 
average) on the warm-up tasks, and the rest of the time (about 
60 minutes) they spent on the actual assignments. The entire 
experiment was time-limited, but a particular task was not. 

Experimental environment.  Each student had access to a computer 
with a web browser, a pen, sheets of paper for private notes, and a 
quick reference guide with descriptions of the proposed program- 
ming constructs (one A4 page). The participants could use simple 
calculators (on their PCs or cell phones) to make the arithmetic 
calculations easier. They were also allowed to browse the slides of 
both the introductory lecture and the review mini-lecture.

(c) Working on assignments. For each task, a piece of code, a set 
of examples (sample input and output) and input data (rela-

form of static text or image (the latter was used for pre-

the results of executing the program without using any de- 
bugger or execution environment—only pen and paper were 
available.  All  of  the  participants  in  the  same  group  were 
given the same code (all codes used are presented in the 
sections to follow). The code for the experimental group was 
based on one of the proposed constructs. The control group 
was presented an equivalent code but without the analysed 
construct.  The predicted results of the computations were 
typed by the subjects into a special web application written 
by one of the authors of the paper. Through that applica- 
tion, the subjects obtained immediate feedback concerning 
the typed-in answer (correct, incorrect). If an answer was 
incorrect, the participant could make another attempt (the 
number of attempts was not limited). The web application 
collected  not only  answers but  also other data: the  num- 
ber of attempts, a timestamp of each attempt made, etc. An 
exemplary  screenshot  of  the  web  application  is  shown  in 
Fig. 1 .

In most cases, the expected answers to the questions associated 
with  the  assignments  were  single  numbers.  To  help  the  partici- 
pants avoid typing errors (e.g. providing letters instead of digits),

In our experiments, we did not analyse the process of predict- 
ing results by the participants, and we did not record any inter- 
mediate results of calculations, just the ﬁnal answers. Therefore, it 
was possible that some of the participants tried to guess the solu- 
tion instead of understanding the code. In the data cleaning phase, 
we applied two simple heuristics to verify if a single observation 
was just a guess: 
• we  checked  if  the  time  of  the  solution  was  suspiciously  too 
short (i.e. much shorter than the solution provided by one of 
the authors), 

• we checked if a participant provided multiple different answers 

at short intervals (i.e. in 10 or fewer seconds). 

The outcome of the cleaning phase was very positive to us: we 

did not identify any case of guessing.

3.3. Threats to validity 

The most important validity threats concerning the experiments 
presented in this paper are threats to external validity .  They ad- 
versely impact the ability to generalise outcomes of the described 
experiments.  Here  are  the  most  essential  factors  raising  doubts 
about external validity: 
• Each end-user programming construct was analysed with only 
one  quite  simple  programming  assignment.  What  if  the  as- 
signments  were  signiﬁcantly  more  complex?  Maybe  the  re- 
sults were even more in favour of the proposed constructs, but 
maybe just the opposite? 

• It  is  not  known  if  the  chosen  programming  assignments  are 
representative  to  the  programming  assignments  junior  man- 
agers would cope with in a real setting or not. In the paper, 
the focus is on numerical-like computations, but maybe other 
types of processing are more popular. 

• One might also doubt if Visual Basic (VB) was the right choice. 
The main argument in favour of VB was the fact that our par- 
ticipants knew the language (they have just ﬁnished a course 
on VB programming). Moreover, the constructs of VB that have 
been used in the experiments are quite general, and they ap- 
pear also in other imperative languages (functions with param- 
eters, arrays, loops). Obviously, the deﬁnitive answer could be 
provided only by experimenting with other languages. 

For the reasons mentioned above, the ﬁndings presented in the 

paper are called Conjuctures . 

Having conclusion validity in mind and potential violation of the 
normality assumption, non-parametric tests have been used (they 
impose less strict requirements on variable distributions, but are 
also less powerful than their parametric counterparts). 

Internal validity and construct validity seem not a problem in the 

case of the described experiments. 

4. Single assignment with exemplary computations 

4.1. Observation 

The  code  of  the  function,  formulated  in  Visual  Basic,  is  pre- 

sented in Fig. 2 a. 

Assume it to be accompanied by the following examples:

 16 

These do not provide insight into the internal properties of the 
function (even if one were to add the ﬁnal values of the variables i 
and Val ). From the understandability standpoint, much more use- 
ful is Fig. 2 b, which presents each variable as a vector of its pre- 
vious values. Perhaps a teacher of an introductory course to pro- 
gramming would ﬁnd this helpful in explaining how the code from 
Fig. 2 a works. However, the approach has one drawback: one has 
to use a structure (two vectors, i and Val ) that does not exist in 
the original program. This seems to be a problem for many end- 
user programmers: it is not easy for them to cope with values that 
are ephemeral, i.e. that disappear by overwriting. Paraphrasing Di- 
jkstra’s famous saying, one can state that in the context of end- 
user programming: 

overwriting is considered harmful. 

4.2. Solution 

The above problem could be solved with the application of the 
single-assignment approach to programming. Using the terminol- 
ogy of imperative languages, the essence of single assignment can 
be described in the following way: 

each variable is assigned a value exactly once. 

Thus,  if  a  code  fragment  has  the  single  assignment  property, 
then none of the variables are overwritten, i.e. nothing disappears, 
and the ﬁnal values of the variables explain very well how the pro- 
gram worked. 

Single assignment is a fundamental property of functional lan- 
guages ( Appel, 1998; McGraw et al., 1985; Scholz, 2003 ), although 
it was invented as a tool supporting code optimisation for imper- 
ative languages. In the latter case, it is a property of intermediate 
representation and appears in two forms: static ( Kelsey, 1995 , most 
popular) or dynamic ( Vanbroekhoven et al., 2007 ). 

In imperative languages (like C or VB) single assignment can be 
used as a style of programming. If there are many re-assignments 
to a variable, one can replace that variable by a one-dimensional 
array. For instance, the code of Fig. 2 a could be transformed into 
the single-assignment version presented in Fig. 3 a. Despite the fact 
that the latter code is longer and more complex (e.g. in the sense 
of  Halstead  (1977)  measures  which  take  into  consideration  the 
number of operators and operands to calculate the volume and the 
diﬃculty of the code), it seems to be easier to explain, especially if 
accompanied by values of the arrays (see Fig. 3 b). A disadvantage 
of this approach might be greater memory consumption (an array 
instead of a single variable). Fortunately, existing code optimisation 
techniques would easily replace that array by a single variable. 

It  is  widely  accepted  that  examples  help  to  understand  vari- 
ous kinds of formulae, including program code. For instance, exem- 
plary computations lie at the heart of the concept of live program- 
ming ( Hancock, 2003; Hermans and van der Storm, 2016; Schus- 
ter and Flanagan, 2015 ): a combination of input data and a live 
programming  environment  provides  programmers  with  immedi- 
ate and continuous feedback about how their modiﬁcations to the 
code affect program execution ( McDirmid, 2007 ). 

However,  pure  examples  do  not  help  very  much.  Consider  a 

simple function with the purpose described below: 

Function 1 (Power) . For a given a and n calculate the n -th power 
of a , i.e. a 

n .

The results presented above justify the following conjecture: 

Conjecture 1. Programs based on single assignment with exemplary 
computations seem to be easier to understand for end-user program- 
mers than their counterparts based on overwriting. 

5. Iterations: Imperative vs. data-driven 

5.1. Observation 

A  single-assignment  program  (see  e.g.  Fig.  3 a),  although  eas- 
ier to understand (as suggested by Conjecture 1 ), still seems far- 
removed from what would be expected by end-user programmers. 
Above  all,  it  lacks  visualisation.  Even  though  exemplary  compu- 
tations present  intermediate results,  there  is no  explicit  connec- 
tion between the output data and the code used to calculate it, 
i.e. which cell was written by which statement. End-user program- 
mers have to make an effort to analyse the code and create this 
connection for themselves. 

5.2. Solution 

To help with this, we decided to introduce two kinds of arrays: 
• index array — this is an array which is a copy of an existing 
array (e.g. input array), or an array of values deﬁned by three 
parameters: the value of the ﬁrst item, an expression describing 
how to get the next item, and an expression deﬁning the last 
item of the array; 

• value array — this is an array associated with some index array 
and is deﬁned by two expressions: one describing the value of 
the ﬁrst item, and the other deﬁning how to compute the next 
item. The size of a value array equals the size of the associated 
array. 

Both index and value arrays are based on single assignment, i.e. 
a  value  is  assigned  to  each  of  their  items  only  once.  This  helps 
to visualise iterative computations. We propose the following rules 
for visualisation: 

Fig. 2.  A piece of code in Visual Basic (a) and its exemplary computation (b) for 
Power(2, 4), which shows successive values of the variables i and Val . 

Fig. 3.  A single-assignment version of the function from Fig. 2 a and its exemplary 
computation for Power(2, 4). 

Fig. 4.  A function which returns the value of a polynomial when the array of co- 
eﬃcients and the value of the variable are given. The code overwrites the local 
variables (control group). 

• initial items in both index and value arrays are presented with 
a white background colour, and non-initial items are presented 
with a background colour chosen by the programmer; 

• items of a value array that have been computed using the same 

expression have the same background colour; 

• names  of  index  and  value  arrays  are  presented  with  a  grey 

background (see Fig. 8 ). 

Moreover, as regards the expressions used to calculate values, 

we apply the following principles: 

• the dollar symbol ($) denotes the value of the previous item in 

the array; 

• to enhance readability, names of array items appearing in ex- 
pressions are presented with the same background colour as in 
the array ’declaration’ (see Fig. 9 ); 

• several operators are deﬁned to work on arrays and used within 

expressions (see Tab. 3 ).

The understandability of each user-deﬁned function is enhanced 
by accompanying its code by at least one exemplary computation: 

• code  and  exemplary  computations  are  displayed  on  separate 

cards; 

• each card (containing code or an exemplary computation) con- 
sists  of  three  vertically  arranged  parts:  input  parameters,  a 
working area containing index and value arrays, and result. 

A code card together with related cards of examples forms a 
’board’ (to some extent, a computation resembles a board game). 
In this paper, this style of representing algorithms is referred to as 
Board Programming. In Fig. 8 a board-programming version of the 
Power function of Fig. 3 a is presented. The board consists of one 
card of code and two cards of examples.

Examples in Board Programming can be easily transformed to 
test cases. End users are able to provide an expected value of a 
function for given arguments. If the value differs from the actual 
result, the test case fails and is marked red; otherwise, it is marked 
green (see Fig. 10 ). Any change to the code immediately causes the 
test cases to be recalculated. 

5.3. Experimental evaluation 

The impact of Board Programming, i.e. single assignment with 
exemplary computations and making use of data-driven arrays, on 
the understandability of the Polynomial function was evaluated in 
the following experiment, conducted within a single session in the 
academic year 2014/2015. 

Assignment.  There  were  70  students  participating  in  the  experi- 
ment (31 in the control group and 39 in the experimental group). 
The participants were given the code of a function computing the 
value of a given polynomial (see Fig. 2 ). The control group received 
the function formulated in Visual Basic (see Fig. 4 ) and the exper- 
imental group in Board Programming ( Fig. 9 ). 

Results.  As shown in Fig. 11 , the participants in the experimental 
group, on average, completed their tasks faster than those in the 
control group. The median prediction times ( T ) were 4 4 4 and 1213 
seconds respectively for the two groups (mean: 470 and 1250 sec.; 

The cancellation ratio ( C ) was 71% for the control group, while 
all of the participants in the experimental group solved the task in 
the given time (see Fig. 12 and Table 4 ). The difference was statis- 
tically signiﬁcant (p-value

INTRODUCTION

Ontologies play a key role in realizing the full power of e-
technology. Ontologies allow for machine-understand-
able semantics of data, and facilitate the search, exchange,
and integration of knowledge for B2B (business-to-busi-
ness) and B2C (business-to-consumer) e-commerce. On-
tology is defined as “the specification of shared knowl-
edge” (Waterson & Preece, 1999). By using semantic data,
the usability of e-technology can be facilitated. There are
several languages like XML (extensible markup language),
RDF  (resource  description  framework),  RDFS  (RDF
schema), DAML+OIL, and OWL. Many tools have been
developed for implementing metadata of ontologies using
these languages. However, current tools have problems
with interoperation and collaboration. The primary goal of
this survey is to introduce and understand several tools
through  their  use.  Therefore,  we  can  develop  a  new
generation of tools that not only support more capabili-
ties, but also solve the problems of current tools.

BACKGROUND

Ontology tools can be applied to all stages of the ontol-
ogy life cycle including the creation, population, imple-
mentation, and maintenance of ontologies (Polikoff, 2003).
An  ontology  can  be  used  to  support  various  types  of
knowledge management including knowledge retrieval,
storage, and sharing (Pundit & Bishr, 1999). In one of the
most popular definitions, an ontology is “the specifica-
tion of shared knowledge” (Waterson & Preece, 1999). For
a  knowledge-management  system,  an  ontology  can  be
regarded as the classification of knowledge. Ontologies
are different from traditional keyword-based search en-
gines in that they are metadata, able to provide the search
engine with the functionality of semantic matching. On-
tologies are able to search more efficiently than traditional
methods. Typically, an ontology consists of hierarchical
descriptions of important concepts in a domain and the
descriptions of the properties of each concept.

Traditionally,  ontologies  are  built  by  both  highly
trained knowledge engineers and domain specialists who
may not be familiar with computer software. Ontology
construction  is  a  time-consuming  and  laborious  task.
Ontology tools also require users to be trained in knowl-
edge representation and predicate logic.

 XML is not suited to describe machine-understand-
able documents and interrelationships of resources in an
ontology (Gunther, 1998). Therefore, the W3C has recom-
mended the use of RDF, RDFS, DAML+OIL, and OWL.
Since then, many tools have been developed for imple-
menting the metadata of ontologies by using these lan-
guages.

MAIN  THRUST  OF  THE  ARTICLE

There are several ontology languages like XML, RDF(S),
DAML+OIL, and OWL that are used to implement tools
for implementing the metadata of ontologies.

Protégé 2000

Protégé  (Noy,  Sintek,  Decker,  Crubezy,  Fergerson,  &
Musen,  2001)  is  developed  by  Stanford  Medical
Informatics. With Protégé, a user can construct domain
ontologies, customize data entry forms, and enter data.
Protégé has an extensible plug-in architecture, allowing
users  to  add  functionality  by  using  plug-ins.  Hence,
Protégé can be easily extended to use knowledge-based
embedded  applications.  Tables  and  diagrams  are  con-
structed  using  graphical  widgets.  However,  new  basic
types cannot be added in Protégé.

Protégé 2000 assumes that knowledge-based systems
are usually very expensive to build and maintain because
knowledge-based system development is done by a team
including both developers and domain experts who may
be less familiar with computer software. Protégé 2000
guides developers and domain experts through the pro-
cess of system development. Developers can reuse do-
main  ontologies  and  problem-solving  methods  with

Ontology Development Tools for Ontology-Based Knowledge Management

Protégé 2000, shortening the time for development and
program maintenance. One domain ontology that solves
different problems can be used in several applications,
and different ontologies can use the same problem-solv-
ing methods.

OilEd

OilEd (Bechhofer, Horrocks, Goble, & Stevens, 2001) is
developed by the Information Management Group of the
CS Department at the University of Manchester, United
Kingdom. OilEd is an OIL editor that allows a user to create
and edit OIL ontologies. OilEd is primarily intended to
demonstrate  the  use  of  DAML+OIL,  but  it  does  not
support a full ontology-development environment. OilEd
does not support many activities such as the creation of
large-scale  ontologies,  versioning,  augmentation,  and
the migration and integration of ontologies that are in-
volved in ontology construction. OilEd has no extensibil-
ity, but arbitrary class expressions, primitive and defined
classes, and concrete-type expressions can be used.

HTML (hypertext markup language) document.

RDFedt is a textual language editor. It is not a Java
program, is not platform independent, and works only on
Windows.

OntoLingua

OntoLingua (Fikes, Farquhar, & Rice, 1997) is developed
by the Knowledge Systems Lab of Stanford University. It
provides a user-distributed collaborative environment, a
suite of ontology-authoring tools, and a library of modu-
lar, reusable ontologies. It also supports a World Wide
Web  (WWW)  interface  and  translation  into  different
formats. OntoLingua is an ontology library and server
that can be accessed with a traditional Web browser. By
assembling and extending the ontologies obtained from
the library and tools in OntoLingua, authorization can be
provided. Using Chimaera, the taxonomy is reorganized
and name conflicts in the knowledge base are resolved.
Multiple users can use OntoLingua via write-only locking
and user access-level assignment.

Apollo

OntoEdit

Apollo  (Koss,  2002)  is  developed  by  the  Knowledge
Media  Institute  of  Open  University,  United  Kingdom.
Apollo allows a user to model an ontology with basic
primitives  such  as  classes,  instances,  functions,  rela-
tions, and so forth. The internal model is a frame system
based  on  the  OKBC  protocol.  The  knowledge  base  of
Apollo consists of hierarchically organized ontologies.
Ontologies can be inherited from other ontologies and can
be  used  as  if  they  were  their  own  ontologies.  Every
ontology has a default ontology, which includes all primi-
tive classes. Each class can create a number of instances,
and an instance inherits all slots of the class. Each slot
consists of a set of facets. Apollo can be extended with
plug-ins, but it does not support collaborative working.

RDFedt

RDFedt is developed by Jan Winkler of Germany. RDFedt
allows a user to build complex and structured RDF and
RSS (RDF site summary) documents. It provides an over-
view of complex data structures with element trees. Also,
it allows a user to test data and to give comments and error
messages with the help of additional functions.

RDFedt supports RDF, RDFS, and Dublin core ele-
ments. RSS 1.0 provides modules like aggregation, nota-
tion, content, cut, organization, change of page, thread-
ing, and so forth. RSS 0.91 supports declaration and levels
of  styles  in  XML,  sets  of  imported  elements,  and  the
automatic generation of an RDF-based linked list from an

OntoEdit (Sure, Angele, & Staab, 2003) is developed by
Ontoprise of Germany. There are freeware and profes-
sional versions. Our survey focused on freeware. OntoEdit
offers export interfaces to all major ontology-representa-
tion languages and has a flexible plug-in framework. This
feature  allows  a  user  to  customize  the  tool  in  a  user-
friendly fashion. Several functions are modularized, so it
can be easily extended.

An ontology requirements-specification document
describing what an ontology should support is needed for
ontology  development.  According  to  the  ontology  re-
quirements-specification  document,  an  ontology  engi-
neer determines relevant concepts and their hierarchical
structure in the ontology. OntoEdit can be used in this
phase using two plug-ins, OntoKick and Mind2Onto5, for
metaontology description with the automatic calculation
of statistic information.

WebODE

WebODE (Arpirez, Corcho, Fernandez-Lopez, & Gomez-
Perez, 2001; Corcho, Fernandez-Lopez, Gomez-Perez, &
Vicente, 2002) is developed by the Technical School of
Computer Science in Madrid, Spain. It was made to use
and test the methontology methodology. The motivation
of WebODE is to support an integrated ontological engi-
neering  workbench,  which  has  three  activity  groups:
ontology-development,  -management,  and  -population
activities; ontology middleware services; and ontology-

2

Ontology Development Tools for Ontology-Based Knowledge Management

based application development. WebODE supports var-
ied ontology-related services and most of the activities
involved in the ontology-development process. It is not an
isolation tool for ontology development. The WebODE
architecture consists of three tiers. The first tier provides
the user interface, the second tier provides the business
logic, and the third tier consists of the data.

KAON

KAON (Volz, Oberle, Staab, & Motik, 2003) is developed
by the FZI Research Center and the AIFB Institute of the
University of Karlsruhe, Germany. KAON is designed to
manage business applications. KAON has two user-level
applications: OiModeler and KAON PORTAL. All other
modules except for these two applications are for software
development. OiModeler is an ontology editor for ontol-
ogy creation and maintenance. We can navigate and search
ontologies with a Web browser using KAON PORTAL.
KAON  supports  scalable  and  efficient  reasoning  with
ontologies; RDFS extension with symmetric, transitive,
and inverse relations; and metamodeling using axiom pat-
terns.

ICOM

ICOM is developed by Free University of Bozen-Bolzano,
Italy.  The  purpose  of  the  development  of  ICOM  is  to
provide a freeware conceptual modeling tool that can be
used for knowledge representation in database and ontol-
ogy  design.  It  is  useful  in  the  conceptual  modeling  of
databases  and  the  design  of  various  ontologies.  It  sup-
ports interontology mapping with the GUI (graphical user
interface). ICOM is created with Java 1.2 and can be run on
Linux and Windows machines. The CORBA protocol with
the FaCT description logic server is used for ICOM com-
munication.

DOE

DOE (Differential Ontology Editor; Isaac, Troncy, & Malais,
2003) is developed by the National Audiovisual Institute
in France. It follows a methodology proposed by Bruno
Bachimont. DOE is not developed for full ontology devel-
opment, so many activities in traditional ontology con-
struction are not supported. DOE allows a user to attach
a lexical definition to concepts and relations and justify
their hierarchy.

DOE has problems importing Dublin core metadata. In
DOE, interoperability can be applied using both RDFS and
OWL, and concepts cannot be defined intentionally with
constraints.  Individuals  cannot  be  imported  during  the
running of WebODE.

WebOnto



WebOnto (Domingue, Motta, & Corcho Garcia, 1999),
developed  by  the  Knowledge  Media  Institute  of  the
Open University in England, supports the collaborative
browsing,  creation,  and  editing  of  ontologies,  repre-
sented in the knowledge-modeling language OCML with-
out  suffering  from  the  interface  problems.  WebOnto
attempts  to  be  easy  to  use  and  yet  scalable  to  large
ontologies. The main features of WebOnto are the man-
agement of ontologies using a graphical interface, the
automatic generation of instance-editing forms from class
definitions, the inspection of elements taking into ac-
count  the  inheritance  of  properties,  and  consistency
checking and support for collaborative work using broad-
casting and receiving and making annotations. WebOnto
consists of a Java-based central server and clients.

Medius Visual Ontology Modeler

Medius  Visual  Ontology  Modeler  (VOM)  is  a  UML-
based  ontology-modeling  tool  that  enables  ontology
development and management for use in collaborative
applications and interoperability, and is available as an
add-on  to  the  Rational  Rose  Enterprise  Edition.  It  is
developed by Sandpiper Software. It has a set of ontol-
ogy-authoring wizards that create and maintain the re-
quired UML model elements for the user, substantially
reducing construction errors and inconsistencies. That
is to say, it supports limited consistency checking.

LinKFactory  Workbench

LinKFactory Workbench (Deray & Verheyden, 2003) is
designed  for  very  large  medical  ontologies.  The
LinKFactory  client-server  structure  is  an  information
system constructed using a three-tier architecture. First,
LinKFactory Workbench is a client application on the
user side to manage the LinKBase ontology database.
Second, LinKFactory is the server interface that receives
and answers user requests, holds the business logic, and
requests data using the application-server tier. Third, the
data layer accesses the underlying database. This data-
base contains all information (user information, ontol-
ogy contents, and maintenance information).

K-Infinity

K-Infinity is a tool developed by Intelligent Views, a
German company, for the creation, maintenance, and use
of a knowledge network. It is a knowledge editor with
broad support for object-oriented knowledge modeling.

FUTURE  TRENDS

There are still some research challenges. Ontology tools
have to support more expressive power and scalability

with a large knowledge base, and reasoning in querying
and matching. Also, they need to support the use of high-

There are also research and applications about dy-

Research  on  ontology-integration  tasks  in  B2B  e-

CONCLUSION

So far, we have described 14 ontology tools. All of these
tools are ontology-development tools. To compare each
tool’s  features,  we  have  chosen  the  tools  with  similar
purpose. Of course, there are many other tools that have
different purposes. For example, Chimaera, FCA-merge,
and PROMPT are ontology-merge and -integration tools.
AeroDAML, COHSE, MnM, and OntoAnnotate are on-
tology-annotation tools. Sesame, Inkling, rdfDB, Redland,
jena,  and  cerebra  are  ontology-storing  and  -querying
tools.

Several  important  aspects  when  we  analyze  tools
exist. Most of the tools are moving toward Java platforms
and extensible architectures as well. Interoperability and
storage  in  databases  are  still  weak  points  of  ontology
tools.

Polikoff (2003) used Protégé 2000, OilEd, and OntoEdit
to test the interoperability of ontology tools. For example,
plain RDFS from OilEd could be used in OilEd and Protégé
2000, but it was not working well in OntoEdit. Plain RDFS
from Protégé 2000 could be used in Protégé 2000 and OilEd
version 19990303, but it could not be used in OntoEdit.
Also, standard Oil RDFS from Protégé 2000 and OWL from
OilEd could not be used in all tools (OilEd, Protégé 2000,
and OntoEdit). DAML+OIL from OilEd could be used in
OilEd and OntoEdit with minor problems, but it could not
be used in Protégé 2000. Interoperability with other ontol-
ogy-development tools, -merging tools, and databases,
as well as translations to and from some ontology lan-
guages, is an important factor in order to integrate ontolo-
gies in applications. However, there are few comparative
studies about the quality of all translators, the possibility
of exchanging ontologies between different tools, and the
loss of knowledge in the translation processes.

In case of storage, only a few of the surveyed tools
use  databases  for  storing  ontologies:  LinKFactory,
OntoEdit  Professional  Version,  Protégé  2000,  and
WebODE. Also, only a few have backup-management
functionality.

Although  a  lot  of  similar  ontology  tools  exist  for
ontology creation, they do not interoperate well and do
not cover all the activities of the ontology life cycle. The
lack of interoperability between all these tools creates

  5

Ontology Development Tools for Ontology-Based Knowledge Management

important problems, for example, when we integrate an
ontology into the ontology library of a different tool, or
when two ontologies built using different tools or lan-
guages are integrated using merging tools.

SPARK: Adapting Keyword Query to Semantic

Search

Qi Zhou, Chong Wang, Miao Xiong, Haofen Wang and Yong Yu

Apex Data and Knowledge Management Lab??

Department of Computer Science and Engineering,

Shanghai JiaoTong University, 200240, Shanghai, P.R.China,

{jackson, wangchong, xiongmiao, whfcarter, yyu}@apex.sjtu.edu.cn

Abstract. Semantic search promises to provide more accurate result
than present-day keyword search. However, progress with semantic search
has been delayed due to the complexity of its query languages. In this pa-
per, we explore a novel approach of adapting keywords to querying the
semantic web: the approach automatically translates keyword queries
into formal logic queries so that end users can use familiar keywords to
perform semantic search. A prototype system named ‘SPARK’ has been
implemented in light of this approach. Given a keyword query, SPARK
outputs a ranked list of SPARQL queries as the translation result. The
translation in SPARK consists of three major steps: term mapping, query
graph construction and query ranking. Speciﬁcally, a probabilistic query
ranking model is proposed to select the most likely SPARQL query. In
the experiment, SPARK achieved an encouraging translation result.

1 Introduction

In the next stage of web revolution, termed the semantic web, web resources will
be made available with various kinds of metadata described in ontologies1. Cor-
respondingly, many semantic query languages (e.g. RQL [1], RDQL 2, SquishQL
[2] and SPARQL 3) have been proposed for querying these ontologies. However,
in order to use these semantic query languages, end users have to master com-
plex formal logic representations and be familiar with the underlying ontologies.
This has become a critical gap between semantic search and end users [3][4].
Meanwhile, most users have been accustomed to the traditional keyword search
for years. Therefore, it is valuable to enable the users to carry out semantic
search by inputting keyword query. However, keyword query is very diﬀerent
from semantic search. To adapt keyword query to semantic search, we have to
overcome the following obstacles: 1) Vocabulary Gap: Casual web users usually

?? This work is funded by IBM China Research Lab.
1 In this paper, ontology refers to a knowledge base (KB) that includes concepts,

relations, instances and instance relations that together model a domain.

2 http://www.w3.org/Submission/RDQL/
3 http://www.w3.org/TR/rdf-sparql-query/

have no knowledge of the underlying ontology, so the words in their queries may
be quite diﬀerent from those in the ontology. 2) Lack of Relation: Relations
between concepts/instances are required to be explicitly stated in formal logic
queries, which are often missing in keyword queries [5]. How to automatically
discover these missing relations becomes a big problem. 3) Query Ranking: Due
to the ambiguity of keyword query, there may be multiple formal queries pro-
duced from one keyword query. How to rank these queries is a big challenge
[6].

Faced with these diﬃculties, we present our novel approach in SPARK sys-
tem. SPARK can automatically translate keyword queries into corresponding
SPARQL queries under the domain ontology, with the aim of adapting keyword
query to semantic search. The main translation steps are: term mapping, query
graph construction and query ranking. Term mapping maps the terms of a key-
word query to the resources of the knowledge base to narrow the vocabulary
gap. After that, query graph construction links the mapped resources so that
the missing relations and concepts can be obtained and a complete query graph
can be constructed. Finally, the probabilistic query ranking model estimates the
most likely SPARQL query among all the candidate queries. In this way, the end
users can keep the habit of typing keywords and querying the semantic web data
transparently, which increases the social utilization of semantic search. From the
evaluation of 750 various keyword queries over three ontologies, SPARK achieved
an encouraging MRR 4 score of 0.677.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 deﬁnes the problem
of formal query construction. Section 3 details the main steps of formal query
construction in SPARK. The implementation and experimental result are pre-
sented in Section 4. Section 5 outlines the related work. We give the conclusion
and future work in the last section.

2 From Keywords to Formal Query

Answering many kinds of semantic query can be formulated as a problem of
ﬁnding a group of objects which are connected by certain relationships and
restrictions. In ontology, a semantic query is equal to a query graph with con-
strained object nodes and property arcs. An example query is “Find all the states
that the mississippi river runs through and border texas” querying the geography
ontology (Fig. 1). It can be rewritten as an equivalent conjunctive formal logic
expression:
?x ← (?x, is, State)∩(Mississippi River, runThrough, ?x)∩(?x, border, Texas)

where class ‘State’, instance ‘Mississippi River’ and ‘Texas’ are ontological re-
strictions on nodes while ‘border’ and ‘runThrough’ are the required connecting
arcs in the pattern. ‘?x’ is the variable passing these restrictions on the query. So
we can reduce the problem of translating keyword queries into formal queries to

For example, assume that a web user intends to express the information need
“Show me the states which the mississippi river runs through? ”. He may type
